Five papers, explained with their slides

Delgado, Nall & Selvin (2020), Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience 13:10

Pin1 binding to phosphorylated PSD-95 regulates the number of functional excitatory synapses

Brain cells talk across synapses (tiny junctions). On the receiving side, a scaffold protein called PSD-95 holds the receptors that catch the chemical signal. This paper asks what makes PSD-95 leave a synapse. Answer: a chain of events. A tag is added to PSD-95, an enzyme called Pin1 grabs that tag, PSD-95 loses a fatty "anchor," and fewer working synapses remain.

Background you need first

The big idea. A synapse is only as good as the receptors sitting in it, and receptors are held in place by scaffold proteins. PSD-95 is the most abundant scaffold on the receiving ("postsynaptic") side of excitatory synapses. If PSD-95 leaves, the synapse weakens or disappears. Learning and forgetting (plasticity) involve adding or removing PSD-95, so the cell must have a way to control it. This paper finds one control switch.

The chain of events (read this first, the rest are details). (1) A kinase adds a phosphate to PSD-95 at T19 and S25. (2) Pin1 recognizes the phosphate through its WW domain and binds. (3) While Pin1 sits there, PSD-95 cannot get its palmitate (fatty) anchor on cysteines 3 and 5. (4) Without the anchor PSD-95 is not held at the synapse, so fewer PSD-95 clusters, fewer spines and fewer working synapses remain. (5) The synapses that survive look normal, so Pin1 controls how many synapses, not how strong each one is.

Why palmitoylation? Palmitoylation is reversible: enzymes add palmitate and others remove it. That cycling lets a cell tune how much PSD-95 sticks to the membrane quickly. Blocking Pin1-binding sites or boosting palmitate should therefore rescue the effect, which is exactly what the authors test.

Key terms in this paper
Synapse
the junction where one neuron signals to the next
Excitatory synapse
a synapse that makes the next neuron more likely to fire; uses the chemical glutamate
PSD-95
a scaffold protein that holds glutamate receptors in place on the receiving side
AMPA and NMDA receptors (AMPARs, NMDARs)
the two main glutamate receptors; AMPARs carry fast signals, NMDARs let calcium in
Phosphorylation (T19, S25)
a kinase enzyme attaches a phosphate tag to a specific amino acid; T19 is threonine 19, S25 is serine 25
Pin1
an enzyme that reads phosphate tags and flips the shape of the protein next to a proline
WW domain
the part of Pin1 that grabs tagged proteins; separate from the part that flips shapes (the isomerase domain)
Palmitoylation
attaching a fatty acid (palmitate) to a protein, like a greasy anchor that keeps PSD-95 in the membrane
Overexpression / knockdown (shRNA)
making cells produce extra of a protein / turning its production down
mEPSC
a tiny electrical blip from one packet of glutamate; counting blips measures how many working synapses a cell has

Top findings, slide by slide

1. Pin1 docks onto the phosphorylated N-terminus of PSD-95

Plain version: Pin1 only sticks to PSD-95 after PSD-95 is tagged.

Why they did this: A good claim needs a mechanism, so first they show Pin1 and PSD-95 physically meet, and only at tagged sites. The experiments compare tagged vs untagged forms, which is the control that proves the phosphate matters.

How to read this slide

Western blots after co-immunoprecipitation. Each lane is a sample; bands show which proteins were pulled down. Look for bands for PSD-95 and phospho-T19 in the Pin1 pull-down.

What it shows

When Pin1 is pulled out of cell or brain extract, PSD-95 (including its phosphorylated form) comes with it. Proteins that co-purify are in the same complex, at least indirectly.

How to read this slide

Surface plasmon resonance sensorgrams. The y-axis (response units) rises as Pin1 flows over the chip and sticks, and falls when washed off. The peptides shown are the sequences around T19 and S25, with or without a phosphate.

What it shows

Pin1 binds the phosphorylated peptides far better than the unphosphorylated ones, so the binding is direct and depends on the phosphate tag. This points to the WW domain, which reads phospho-serine/threonine followed by proline.

Putting it together: Pin1 is a reader of phosphorylation. That makes it a bridge between kinase signaling (activity-dependent tagging) and the physical stability of PSD-95.

Full detail from the paper

The N-terminus (the start of the protein chain) of PSD-95 has two sites, T19 and S25, that kinases tag with phosphate. Many PSD-95 molecules are already tagged there at rest. Pin1 uses its WW domain to grab tagged sites. The slides show two tests. In a co-immunoprecipitation (pull one protein out of a cell extract with an antibody and see what comes along), Pin1 brought PSD-95 with it. In surface plasmon resonance (a chip detects binding as mass sticks to it; a rising signal means binding, a falling one means release), Pin1 bound the phosphorylated T19 and S25 peptides and not the untagged ones. The paper says this binding work is "in review," so the slides are the direct evidence.

2. Pin1 removes the palmitate anchor, so PSD-95 clusters and spines are lost

Plain version: more Pin1 means less anchored PSD-95, fewer spines, and fewer synapses.

Why they did this: Binding alone does not show a consequence, so next they ask what binding does to the PSD-95 anchor. They use a reporter that glows only when PSD-95 is palmitoylated, then test with a mutant lacking the tag sites and a drug that preserves palmitate.

How to read this slide

HEK cells with green hPF11 reporter and red PSD-95. Rows: DMSO (solvent control) vs Palmostatin B (stops palmitate removal). Columns: no Pin1 vs Pin1. Arrows point to green clusters where PSD-95 is anchored.

What it shows

Pin1 nearly eliminates clusters (1.00 to 0.04). Palmostatin B boosts control clusters (1.49) but Pin1 still holds them low (0.14). The authors read this as Pin1 binding dominating over the drug. With N3A (cannot be phosphorylated) Pin1 had much less power after Palmostatin B, so the tag sites are needed for much of the block.

How to read this slide

Neuron dendrites with hPF11-GFP, comparing control vs Pin1. The graph compares reporter brightness in spines to the neighboring dendrite (an enrichment ratio).

What it shows

In control neurons hPF11 is concentrated in spines (ratio 1.54; about 90% of spines enriched). With Pin1 it is spread evenly (0.93; fewer than 20% enriched). Pin1 also lowered PSD-95 clusters per 30 µm (about 26 to 16) and spine density (0.77 to 0.57 per µm). A mutant Pin1 that cannot flip protein shape gave the same drop (0.53), so physical binding is enough.

Putting it together: Pin1 acts as a "do not anchor" sign on PSD-95. Overexpressing PSD-95 restored cluster numbers, which means the problem is how much anchored PSD-95 is available, not a general loss of other proteins.

Full detail from the paper

Palmitoylation of cysteines 3 and 5 is what keeps PSD-95 stable in the synapse. To see it, the authors used hPF11 (a glowing GFP-tagged antibody fragment that binds only anchored PSD-95). In HEK cells (a common lab cell line), adding Pin1 cut hPF11 clusters from 1.00 to 0.04 (normalized to control). Palmostatin B (a drug that blocks removal of palmitate) raised control clusters to 1.49 but Pin1 still held them to 0.14, so Pin1 dominates. With the N3A mutant (T19, S25 and S35 swapped for alanine so they cannot be tagged), Palmostatin B worked much better (1.32 with Pin1 vs 2.01 without). In neurons, Pin1 dropped hPF11 enrichment in spines from 1.54 to 0.93, PSD-95 clusters per 30 µm from about 26 to 16, and spines per µm from 0.77 to 0.57. A mutant Pin1 that cannot flip shapes (C113S) did the same (0.53), so binding, not shape-flipping, is what matters.

3. Fewer working synapses, but the remaining ones are normal strength

Plain version: Pin1 changes how many synapses there are, not how strong each one is.

Why they did this: Fewer clusters and spines should mean fewer working synapses. They test electrically, and ask whether surviving synapses are weaker or just fewer. Using both AMPAR and NMDAR readouts shows the effect is general.

How to read this slide

Raw current traces from a neuron (each downward spike is one mEPSC) with graphs for frequency and amplitude, EGFP control vs Pin1.

What it shows

Frequency drops from 6.45 to 4.23 Hz but amplitude stays similar (17.2 vs 14.3 pA, p = 0.11). Frequency reflects how many working synapses (or release events) there are; amplitude reflects the strength of each. So Pin1 reduces synapse number, not synapse strength.

How to read this slide

Pin1 knockdown with two shRNAs: calcium events in single spines from NMDARs, plus a Western blot showing Pin1 was reduced.

What it shows

Removing Pin1 roughly doubles NMDAR calcium signal size (about 2.3 vs 1.0) and, for one shRNA, event frequency (0.13 vs 0.05). The reverse manipulation gives the reverse result, which strengthens the conclusion that Pin1 is a negative regulator of synapses.

Putting it together: The two directions of manipulation (overexpress and knock down) give opposite results on spines and NMDAR signals. This "gain and loss" logic is stronger than either alone.

Full detail from the paper

With extra Pin1, the frequency of mEPSC blips dropped (6.45 to 4.23 per second) while their size did not change (17.2 vs 14.3 pA, not significant). Fewer synapses, same strength each. The authors also watched single spines light up with calcium (using the sensor GCaMP6s) when NMDARs opened. Turning Pin1 down doubled the NMDAR signal size (about 2.3 vs 1.0) and, with one shRNA, the event rate (0.13 vs 0.05). Extra Pin1 also let AMPARs wander faster (diffusion 0.026 to 0.036 µm²/s). Finally, adding extra PSD-95 restored cluster numbers, which supports that Pin1 works by limiting PSD-95.

Methods that established them

hPF11 palmitoylation reporter

How it works

Cells make PSD-95, a fluorescent antibody-like reporter (hPF11-EGFP) and Pin1 or an empty plasmid. hPF11 only sticks to palmitoylated PSD-95, so green clusters = anchored PSD-95. Researchers count cells with clusters.

Why use it

A reporter lets you see palmitoylation in intact cells, with location, rather than only a bulk blot. Controls: palmitate-blocking drug, N3A mutant, empty vector. The authors say a click-chemistry biochemical assay gave a similar answer (Pin1 down to about 30%), though the data are not shown.

Patch clamp and GCaMP calcium imaging

How it works

A glass pipette seals onto a neuron and records tiny currents. For NMDARs, removing magnesium and blocking AMPARs and action potentials leaves calcium flickers through single spines that GCaMP6s makes visible.

Why use it

Two independent readouts (AMPAR electrical, NMDAR optical) of synaptic function. APV/MK801 abolishing the flickers proves the signals are NMDAR-specific.

Single-particle tracking and super-resolution

How it works

Single GluA2-containing AMPARs are labeled with bright tags and followed frame by frame; the path gives a diffusion coefficient. dSTORM reconstructs images beyond the light diffraction limit so nanodomains (about 70 nm clumps) can be measured.

Why use it

Tests whether Pin1 changes how receptors are organized or how mobile they are, separately from synapse number. Answer: organization unchanged, mobility slightly up.

Check your understanding

Why does the amplitude not change but the frequency does?

Amplitude reflects the response at an individual synapse; frequency reflects how many synapses (or release events) are working. Pin1 removes synapses but leaves the remaining ones intact.

What does the C113S mutant prove?

It cannot flip protein shape (catalytically dead) yet it still reduced spines and PSD-95. So binding through the WW domain, not isomerization, is sufficient. The authors caution that WW binding might shift shape equilibria slowly.

Name a weakness.

Pin1 was overexpressed (about 2-fold) in cultured neurons; the Pin1-binding data are cited as under review; several knockdown effects are modest.

The model slide shows the chain: kinase tags PSD-95, Pin1 binds, palmitate is lost, PSD-95 leaves, spines shrink. Limits: Pin1 was raised only about 2-fold, the biochemical palmitoylation data are "not shown," and most work is in cultured cells.

Treffy et al. (2016), Developmental Neuroscience, DOI 10.1159/000444748

Ephrin-B/EphB signaling is required for normal innervation of lingual gustatory papillae

Taste buds sit in small bumps (papillae) on the tongue and get nerve fibers from a ganglion called the geniculate ganglion. Nerves find the tongue using floating chemical signals, but floating signals cannot explain why fibers stay in exactly the right spot. This paper tests signals that work by touch: ephrins and their Eph receptors.

Background you need first

The big idea. Taste buds are tiny islands of taste cells in a sea of non-taste tongue skin. Nerve fibers must find the islands and stay inside. Floating signals (BDNF attracts, Sema3A repels) get fibers near and into the right area, but they spread through tissue, so they cannot mark a sharp border. Signals fixed on cell surfaces can. Ephrins on one cell touch Eph receptors on the axon and usually repel it.

The logic of the paper. They ask three questions in order. Where and when are ephrin-B and EphB present? (expression). Does ephrin-B alone change how taste neurons grow? (sufficiency, in a dish). Do mice lacking the receptors have defective innervation? (necessity, in the animal). Expression, sufficiency and necessity are the classic three steps to argue a molecule really guides axons.

Why timing matters. Fibers touch the epithelium at E14.5 and enter it by E15.5. Ephrin-B2 appears only from E15.5, after fibers arrive, so it is more likely to limit or stabilize axons inside the papilla than to lure them there.

Key terms in this paper
Innervation
how nerve fibers (axons) connect to a tissue
Fungiform papillae
the mushroom-shaped bumps on the front of the tongue that contain taste buds
Geniculate ganglion
a cluster of nerve cell bodies whose axons (the chorda tympani nerve) carry taste from the front of the tongue
Axon guidance
how growing nerve fibers find their targets using attractive and repulsive signals
Ephrin / Eph receptor
a ligand-receptor pair on cell surfaces; contact between them usually repels a growing axon
Forward signaling
the Eph receptor-bearing cell (here the axon) receives the signal; the reverse is "reverse signaling"
Ephrin-B2 lacZ mouse
a mouse where the ephrin-B2 gene also makes beta-galactosidase, so cells that use it turn blue with a dye
Fc fusion protein
a lab-made ephrin attached to an antibody tail so it can be stuck on a dish
BDNF, NT4
growth factors that keep neurons alive and promote growth; BDNF is made by the papilla and attracts axons
Laminin
a protein in the extracellular matrix, the "glue" between cells, that axons like to grow on
DiI
a fat-soluble red dye that travels along nerve membranes and lights up the whole fiber

Top findings, slide by slide

1. Ephrin-B2 switches on in the tongue just after the nerves arrive; the axons carry EphB receptors

Plain version: the repellent shows up at the right time and place to keep axons in the taste bump.

Why they did this: Before testing function, you must show the right molecules are in the right places at the right times. If ephrin-B2 were absent, a guidance role would be impossible.

How to read this slide

Stained tongue sections. Blue = ephrin-B2 reporter activity at E15.5, E16.5 and E18.5; the bottom row shows antibody staining (red) with nerve fibers in green.

What it shows

At E15.5 ephrin-B2 is faint; by E18.5 it covers the entire tongue surface, and in papillae it is limited to the top layer of cells. Nerve fibers are already inside the papilla before it reaches full strength.

How to read this slide

Antibody staining for EphB1 and EphB2 (red) alongside nerve markers (green: 2H3, GAP43, PGP9.5) in rat and mouse tongue.

What it shows

EphB1 and EphB2 are on the sensory fibers, which means the fibers can "listen" to ephrin-B2 (forward signaling). Fibers also stain for ephrin-B2 in rat, which opens the possibility of reverse signaling.

Putting it together: Ephrin-B2 (repellent) on epithelium and EphB (receptor) on axons are in the right places for a late-stage "stay in your territory" signal. Ephrin-B1 is in tissue under the epithelium, so it may help earlier.

Full detail from the paper

In the mouse, nerve fibers first enter the tongue surface (epithelium) at embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5). The ephrin-B2 reporter showed nothing at E14.5, patches at E15.5, and a continuous layer along the tongue by E18.5, with the fungiform papillae labeled only at their top surface. Ephrin-B1 was nearly absent from the epithelium but present in the tissue beneath it (mesenchyme), so it could guide fibers before they touch the surface. EphB1 and EphB2 receptors were found on tongue nerve fibers and on geniculate neurites grown in a dish. In rat, the nerves also showed ephrin-B2, a species difference the authors note.

2. Ephrin-B1 and B2 repel geniculate nerve fibers, more at higher doses

Plain version: given a choice, taste fibers avoid ephrin and grow less on it.

Why they did this: Expression is only correlation. To show sufficiency, they remove all other cues: geniculate ganglion pieces are grown on surfaces with defined proteins and growth factors.

How to read this slide

Geniculate explants (bright blob) with red neurites growing across vertical stripes. Asterisks mark ephrin-B1 stripes (control, 2, 10 and 40 µg/ml).

What it shows

At low dose, fibers cross stripes freely. At 10 and 40 µg/ml they grow only between ephrin stripes (parallel to them). That avoidance is repulsion.

How to read this slide

Bar graphs of the ratio of fiber length on ephrin vs control stripes (a), and uniform-coating outgrowth, with high vs low laminin.

What it shows

Ratios fall with higher ephrin dose, for B1 and B2, both ages and both growth factors, so the effect does not depend on which neurotrophin feeds the neurons. High laminin raises the ratio, meaning less repulsion.

Putting it together: Laminin concentration changes how axons read ephrin. This suggests a cell integrates multiple cues: sticky matrix helps growth in the papilla core, while ephrin-rich epithelium stops it.

Full detail from the paper

In a stripe assay (a dish coated with alternating stripes of test protein and control protein; you see which stripes the fibers choose), fibers avoided ephrin-B stripes made at 10 and 40 µg/ml but not 2 µg/ml. B1 and B2 worked about equally, at E15 and E18, with either BDNF or NT4 feeding the neurons. When the whole dish was coated evenly, ephrin still shortened growth. Adding more laminin (20 vs 2.5 µg/ml) reduced or removed this effect. So fibers weigh competing signals: laminin-rich tissue deep in the papilla supports growth, while ephrin-rich epithelium discourages it.

3. Mice missing EphB1 and EphB2 lose taste innervation by E17.5

Plain version: without the receptors, fewer nerve fibers end up in the taste bumps.

Why they did this: Finally, necessity: delete the receptors in mice and ask whether innervation breaks. DiI labels the entire nerve, allowing a visual and quantitative comparison.

How to read this slide

Whole tongues labeled with DiI from the ganglion (red) at E13.5, E15.5 and E17.5, wild type left, EphB1/EphB2 double knockout right; insets show a papilla in cross-section with the nerve bundle width marked.

What it shows

Mutants look nearly normal at E13.5 and a bit sparser at E15.5, but at E17.5 far fewer papillae are filled. The bundle under each papilla is thinner (6.5 vs 9.6 µm).

Putting it together: This supports "EphB signaling is needed to maintain innervation," but the receptors were missing everywhere and from the start, so earlier defects cannot be ruled out. Note too that fibers did not overshoot, which a pure repulsion-failure model would predict.

Full detail from the paper

Researchers put DiI at the geniculate ganglion in double knockout embryos (mice with both genes deleted). At E13.5 and E15.5 labeling was slightly reduced, but at E17.5 papillae had much less innervation. The nerve bundle at the base of a papilla was 6.5 ± 0.9 µm wide in knockouts vs 9.6 ± 1.1 µm in controls (p < 0.05, only 2 control and 3 mutant mice). Limits: fibers did not overshoot, and the early reduction means the loss could come from earlier guidance or survival problems, not only from ephrin-B2 in the epithelium.

Methods that established them

Expression mapping (antibodies and the lacZ reporter)

How it works

Tongues are fixed, sliced and incubated with antibodies; tyramide signal amplification makes faint signals visible. In reporter mice, lacZ replaces part of the ephrin-B2 gene so the blue dye marks cells using it.

Why use it

A reporter and an antibody are independent methods; agreement boosts confidence. A "no primary antibody" control checks for background.

Stripe assay

How it works

Silicone channels deposit alternating stripes: first ephrin-Fc (fluorescently labeled), then control Fc. Ganglion pieces are plated and fibers grow for about a day. The ratio of longest fiber on ephrin to longest on control is the readout.

Why use it

It lets fibers choose between two surfaces, so repulsion (avoidance) can be told apart from general toxicity. A uniform coating tests whether ephrin slows growth overall.

DiI tracing in knockout embryos

How it works

DiI crystals placed on the geniculate ganglion of fixed embryos spread along the nerve membranes. Tongues are cleared and imaged; vibratome slices are measured for bundle width.

Why use it

It reveals the whole projection at once. Weakness: small numbers of animals and global knockouts.

Check your understanding

Why isn't ephrin-B2 the attractor that brings fibers to the papilla?

It appears after fibers have already arrived (E15.5 onward) and it repels axons in vitro, so it fits a role in confining or stabilizing fibers.

What does the laminin result add?

It shows the response to ephrin depends on context: more laminin weakens repulsion. Axons weigh multiple cues together.

What would strengthen the in vivo evidence?

Conditional deletion of ephrin-B2 or EphBs only in the epithelium or only in geniculate neurons, plus more animals.

How to present it: expression (the players are in place), then in vitro (ephrin is enough to repel), then in vivo (the receptors are needed). The in vivo result shows EphB1/B2 are needed but does not prove ephrin-B2 acts directly on the axons.

Chen et al. (2026), Nature Communications 17:1285

Integrated stress response inhibition prolongs lifespan of a Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease mouse model by increasing oligodendrocyte survival

Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease (PMD) is caused by faulty myelin protein, PLP. Misfolded PLP builds up in oligodendrocytes (cells that wrap nerves in myelin insulation), stresses them, and they die. A cell stress program called the integrated stress response (ISR) is meant to protect, but here it may do harm. The authors turned the ISR down in the Jimpy mouse to see if it would help.

Background you need first

The big idea. Cells make proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). In PMD the mutant myelin protein PLP misfolds and piles up there, causing ER stress. The cell responds with the unfolded protein response (UPR), whose PERK arm tags a protein called eIF2α with phosphate. Tagged eIF2α blocks the factor eIF2B, which slows overall protein making and turns on stress genes. That whole program is the integrated stress response (ISR).

The twist. In short-lived stress, such as inflammation, the ISR protects oligodendrocytes, and this lab previously showed boosting it helps. But in PMD the mutant protein is made all the time, so the ISR stays on forever. Chronic ISR can push cells to die and also shuts down cholesterol production that myelin needs. So the authors predict the opposite approach, turning the ISR down, will help here.

Two ways to turn it down. Genetic: delete Perk in oligodendrocytes so the sensor never tags eIF2α. Pharmacological: 2BAct and ISRIB lock eIF2B in its active form so that tagged eIF2α cannot inhibit it. Comparing the two reveals what is specific to oligodendrocytes and what is not.

Key terms in this paper
Oligodendrocyte / myelin
the brain cell that makes myelin, the fatty insulation around nerve fibers
PMD / PLP1
Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease, caused by mutations in the PLP1 gene that makes the main myelin protein
Jimpy mouse
a mouse with a Plp1 mutation that models severe PMD; dies about day 21
ER stress / UPR / ISR
misfolded proteins stress the endoplasmic reticulum (protein factory); the UPR and ISR are the cell responses that slow protein making
PERK, eIF2α, eIF2B
PERK is a sensor kinase that tags eIF2α; tagged eIF2α blocks eIF2B and protein production slows
2BAct, ISRIB
drugs that activate eIF2B and thereby switch the ISR off
Perk fl/fl; Olig2-Cre
a genetic trick that deletes the Perk gene only in oligodendrocyte-lineage cells
CHOP, GADD34
ISR proteins: CHOP promotes cell death; GADD34 helps end the ISR
ASPA, MBP, MAG
markers of mature oligodendrocytes and myelin proteins
OPC
oligodendrocyte precursor cell, the dividing stem-like cell that makes new oligodendrocytes
PND
postnatal day, i.e., days since birth

Top findings, slide by slide

1. Deleting Perk in oligodendrocytes extends life by about two weeks and rescues some cells and myelin

Plain version: stopping the stress sensor in the right cells keeps more of them alive.

Why they did this: If the ISR is harmful in Jimpy, removing PERK specifically in oligodendrocytes should keep them alive and the animals should live longer. They also test downstream parts to see which arm of the ISR does the damage.

How to read this slide

Left: survival curves for Jimpy, Jimpy;Perk+/−, Jimpy;Perkfl/fl and Jimpy;Perkfl/fl;Olig2-Cre. Right (RNA-seq panel): ISR gene set up in Jimpy and down with Perk deletion.

What it shows

Perk deletion in oligodendrocytes pushed survival from about 21 to about 33-35 days. The ISR gene set, raised in Jimpy, fell with the deletion, proving the manipulation did turn down the ISR.

How to read this slide

Corpus callosum stains for degenerating axons (DegenoTag), Western blots for MAG and MBP, and myelin-gene expression plots.

What it shows

With Perk deleted, there was less axon damage and more myelin proteins and RNAs. Myelin was still far below normal (EM: about 10% of wild-type axons myelinated), so this is partial rescue, not a cure.

Putting it together: Deleting CHOP or blocking GADD34 did not rescue oligodendrocytes, so the harm does not simply flow through CHOP. This tells you the damaging branch is upstream or CHOP-independent.

Full detail from the paper

Jimpy mice normally die near PND21. With Perk deleted in oligodendrocytes they lived about 33 to 35 days; losing just one copy of Perk helped only a little. At PND19, mature (ASPA-positive) oligodendrocytes in the corpus callosum (the big white-matter bridge between brain halves) rose from near zero to about 100 per mm² (healthy mice about 430), cells dying by apoptosis (programmed cell death, marked by cleaved caspase 3) dropped, and electron microscopy (very high-magnification imaging that can see individual myelin wraps) showed myelinated axons returned to about 10% of normal. Removing downstream ISR parts did not help much: GADD34 mutation did nothing and CHOP deletion added under 2 days.

2. Drugs that switch off the ISR (2BAct, ISRIB) about double lifespan

Plain version: a pill-like treatment, not just genetics, gives an even bigger benefit.

Why they did this: Genetic deletion is a proof of concept. A drug shows therapeutic potential and acts on all cells, so they test whether it works as well and why.

How to read this slide

Survival curve of Jimpy mice on control or 2BAct chow, and a diagram of 2BAct and ISRIB acting on eIF2B.

What it shows

2BAct nearly doubled lifespan (about 18 to about 38 days), better than the genetic approach. Note the treated mice still developed tremors.

How to read this slide

Brain sections showing ASPA (mature oligodendrocytes), EM images of myelin and PDGFRα/Ki67 for OPCs in four groups: WT or Jimpy, with control or 2BAct diet.

What it shows

Treated Jimpy mice kept more mature oligodendrocytes and had some myelinated axons, but OPC numbers and division were not changed by the drug.

How to read this slide

Cultured OPCs from WT or Jimpy pups on days 2 and 3 of differentiation, MBP in green, with DMSO or 5 µM ISRIB.

What it shows

Jimpy cells start to differentiate but then die by day 3. ISRIB keeps MBP-positive cells alive and maturing, and by days 4 and 5 gives more than half the normal number, so the drug acts directly on oligodendrocyte lineage cells.

Putting it together: The in vitro result removes immune cells and the rest of the brain from the picture, showing cell-autonomous rescue. The in vivo result shows it is not only a lab trick.

Full detail from the paper

2BAct was put in chow for the mother and pups. Jimpy survival went from about 18 to about 38 days, more ASPA-positive cells survived, and some myelinated axons became visible. In a dish, OPCs from Jimpy mice made far fewer MBP-positive cells than normal; adding 5 µM ISRIB (a close relative of 2BAct) restored them to more than half of normal by days 4 to 5. Because this happens in isolated cells, the drug works on the oligodendrocytes themselves.

3. The genetic and drug routes work through different mechanisms

Plain version: Perk deletion mainly rescues myelin-building programs; 2BAct mainly calms inflammation.

Why they did this: Both treatments extend life, but are they doing the same thing? RNA-seq measures thousands of genes at once, so the authors can compare molecular footprints.

How to read this slide

Gene set results for 2BAct vs control in Jimpy: down for interferon and immune gene sets, and ISR genes; images of IBA1 (microglia) and GFAP (astrocytes).

What it shows

2BAct dampens neuroinflammation (activated microglia, interferon signatures). The effect on myelin and cholesterol gene sets is smaller than with Perk deletion.

How to read this slide

Oligodendrocyte lineage staging (OPC, pre-myelinating, mature) with images for PDGFRα, BCAS1 and ASPA.

What it shows

Jimpy mice have normal OPC numbers but fewer dividing OPCs. Perk deletion partly restores division and increases newly differentiating and mature cells.

Putting it together: Perk deletion mostly fixes the oligodendrocytes themselves; 2BAct additionally calms the immune response. That is why a drug acting on all cells is not identical to cell-specific deletion.

Full detail from the paper

RNA-seq (reads out which genes are on in a tissue) at PND19 showed Jimpy brains had low myelin and cholesterol-making genes and high ISR genes. Perk deletion restored the myelin and cholesterol sets and lowered the ISR set. 2BAct lowered the ISR set too, but mostly reversed interferon-type inflammation and reduced activated microglia (brain immune cells), with a smaller myelin-gene effect. Perk deletion also partly restored OPC division (Ki67-positive OPCs, 24 up to 51 per mm², healthy 77); 2BAct did not.

Methods that established them

Genetics and survival analysis

How it works

Different crosses place Jimpy with a given ISR-gene mutation. Mice are monitored until moribund. Survival is displayed as Kaplan-Meier curves and compared with the log-rank test.

Why use it

Survival is an unbiased, clinically meaningful outcome. Using several knockouts shows which ISR arms matter. Only males were studied because Jimpy is X-linked.

Immunostaining, EM, blots and qPCR

How it works

Antibodies for ASPA, BCAS1, PDGFRα, Ki67, Casp3 and DegenoTag mark cell types, division, death and damage. EM counts myelinated axons per mm². Western blots and RT-qPCR quantify myelin proteins and RNAs.

Why use it

EM is the gold standard for myelin; blots and qPCR confirm in bulk. Mismatch between MBP staining and EM myelin led the authors to propose microglial MBP signal.

Bulk RNA-seq and gene set analysis

How it works

Reads are aligned to the mouse genome, normalized with limma-voom, and tested for differential expression. Gene sets (e.g., cholesterol biosynthesis, interferon response) are tested together with CAMERA. A set of 95 ISR genes (ISR CLIC) measures pathway activity.

Why use it

It shows pathway-level effects rather than single genes. Limitation: whole-brain RNA mixes cell types, and Jimpy has few oligodendrocytes, so changes are partly changes in cell composition.

Check your understanding

Why would turning the ISR down help here when turning it up helped in inflammation?

Inflammatory stress is temporary so a boosted ISR buys time; mutant PLP is a constant stress, so a chronic ISR becomes harmful and suppresses cholesterol synthesis needed for myelin.

Why compare Perk deletion with 2BAct?

Perk deletion acts only in oligodendrocytes and upstream of eIF2α; 2BAct acts in all cells at eIF2B. Differences (inflammation, OPC division) show cell-type-specific effects.

What does it not show?

It is a mouse model with a non-human mutation, rescue is partial, and the authors flag the unexplained MBP signal.

Limits the authors state: MBP staining rose more than EM myelin did, so some signal may come from microglia; Jimpy is not an actual human mutation; treated mice still shake and die early. Calico scientists are authors and hold a patent on 2BAct.

Hoshino, ..., Rochlin & Yu (2021), Journal of Comparative Neurology 529:3633-3654 (the PDF named Yu_et_al_2013 is this paper)

Ephrin-A3 is required for tonotopic map precision and auditory functions in the mouse auditory brainstem

Your ear sorts sounds by pitch, and the brain keeps that order: nearby pitches are handled by nearby neurons, forming a "map" called tonotopy. This paper asks what builds that map in the first brainstem station for hearing, the cochlear nucleus, and finds a touch-based guidance molecule, ephrin-A3, is needed.

Background you need first

The big idea. The cochlea separates sound by pitch: high frequencies vibrate the base, low frequencies the tip. Auditory nerve fibers keep that order as they enter the brain, so neurons in the cochlear nucleus (CN) are arranged by pitch. This pitch map, tonotopy, is the basis for telling sounds apart. How the fibers find the right place is not well understood.

Borrowing from vision. In the retina-to-superior-colliculus map, opposing gradients of ephrins and Eph receptors steer fibers to the correct position: repulsion is a positioning tool. The authors test whether a similar system sets the pitch map. Ephrin-A3 is a candidate because its levels differ across the CN.

Three levels of evidence. Molecular (does ephrin-A3 repel auditory fibers?), anatomical (does losing it blur the map?), and functional (does the animal hear or discriminate pitch worse?). Together these link a molecule to structure to behavior.

Key terms in this paper
Tonotopy
an orderly map of sound frequency (pitch) across neurons
Cochlea / spiral ganglion neurons
the spiral hearing organ in the ear / the nerve cells that send its signals to the brain
Auditory nerve fibers
the axons of spiral ganglion neurons that carry sound to the brain
Cochlear nucleus (CN, AVCN)
the first brainstem station for hearing; AVCN is its front-bottom part
Apical vs basal
the tip of the cochlea (low pitch) vs its base (high pitch)
Ephrin-A3
a cell-surface guidance molecule that repels axons that carry EphA receptors
Forward signaling
the receptor-carrying axon receives the repulsion signal
Isofrequency band
a strip of neurons that all respond best to one pitch
c-fos
a gene that switches on in active neurons, so c-fos staining shows who responded to a sound
ABR
auditory brainstem response, a scalp-recorded electrical signature of sound traveling up the brainstem; wave II mostly reflects the cochlear nucleus
Pre-pulse inhibition (PPI)
a weak warning cue reduces the startle to a loud noise; better detection of the cue means more reduction

Top findings, slide by slide

1. Ephrin-A3 is arranged along the pitch axis and repels auditory nerve fibers, depending on age

Plain version: the CN has a repellent gradient that can steer incoming fibers.

Why they did this: To steer wiring, a guidance molecule must be present as a gradient and must act on the relevant fibers. They show both with expression stains and an in vitro repulsion test.

How to read this slide

In situ hybridization images of ephrin-A2, -A3, -A4, -A5 and Eph-related stains in the E15.5 and E17.5 cochlear nucleus.

What it shows

Ephrin-A3 mRNA is differentially distributed along the pitch axis during the time fibers arrive, which is what you need for a positioning gradient.

How to read this slide

Stripe assay quantification: ratio of fibers on ephrin-A3 vs control stripes for E15.5 and E17.5 and for apical (low-pitch) or basal (high-pitch) cochlear explants.

What it shows

Ephrin-A3 repels auditory fibers dose-dependently, and the strength depends on embryonic stage. A response that changes with age suggests fibers become sensitized as they mature.

Putting it together: Because ephrin-A3 is a repellent graded across the nucleus, it could limit where fibers of different pitch can terminate and so sharpen the map.

Full detail from the paper

The authors stained the mouse cochlear nucleus at E15.5 and E17.5 for several ephrin-As and found them present in different amounts along the pitch axis. Then in cochlear explants (pieces of ear tissue grown in a dish) they ran a stripe assay (striped coverslips of ephrin vs control; fibers avoid the repellent stripes). Ephrin-A3 stripes repelled auditory fibers, and how strongly depended on the embryo age and on whether the fibers came from the apical or basal cochlea. This is "sufficient" evidence: ephrin-A3 alone can push these fibers.

2. Without ephrin-A3 the map is blurred

Plain version: pitch strips in the brainstem get wider and messier.

Why they did this: The key necessity test: delete ephrin-A3 and ask whether the map is less precise. They check anatomy with tracing and activity with sound-driven gene expression.

How to read this slide

Dye placed at different points of the cochlea labels terminals in the AVCN; plot of the labeled band widths in control vs ephrin-A3 knockout.

What it shows

In mutants, the labeled bands of fibers are broader (less precise) so afferents from a given cochlear point spread over a larger region.

How to read this slide

Brain sections stained for c-fos after exposure to 8 or 16 kHz tones; plots of band width in control vs knockout.

What it shows

Neurons responding to one pitch form wider, blurrier stripes in mutants, so the functional map is also degraded.

Putting it together: The anatomical and functional results agree, which makes the conclusion stronger. Note the map is degraded, not absent: ephrin-A3 is one of several cues.

Full detail from the paper

In ephrin-A3 knockout mice (the gene is deleted), dye traced from different positions on the cochlea landed in a less precise pattern in the AVCN. Mice were also played pure 8 or 16 kHz tones, and c-fos activation bands in the AVCN were wider and less sharp than in normal mice. So both the wiring and the responses are less precise.

3. Hearing is normal, but timing and pitch discrimination suffer

Plain version: mutants hear fine but cannot tell close pitches apart as well.

Why they did this: Does a blurrier brainstem map matter for hearing? They separate sensitivity (can the mouse hear) from discrimination (can it tell pitches apart).

How to read this slide

Auditory brainstem response (ABR) waves for control and knockout, with threshold and latency plots.

What it shows

Thresholds are normal, so the ear is fine, but wave II (cochlear nucleus) is delayed, indicating altered brainstem processing.

How to read this slide

Pre-pulse inhibition results across frequency changes in a background tone: amplitude of startle and percent inhibition in control vs knockout.

What it shows

At small pitch changes mutants inhibit their startle less, which means they detect pitch shifts less well. A degraded map gives poorer pitch discrimination.

Putting it together: Hearing sensitivity is intact while discrimination is impaired. This dissociation shows the map's precision, not the ear, is the problem.

Full detail from the paper

ABR thresholds (the quietest sound that gets a response) were normal, so the ears work. But ABR wave II was delayed, pointing to slower signaling in the cochlear nucleus. In the startle test, mutants were worse at using a small frequency change in a background tone as a warning cue, so they discriminate pitch less well. Together: a sharper map is needed for fine pitch discrimination, not for simply hearing.

Methods that established them

Stripe assay on cochlear explants

How it works

Coverslips are patterned with ephrin-A3-Fc and control stripes; cochlear pieces grow neurites for about a day; the share of fibers on each stripe type is measured at multiple doses and ages.

Why use it

It isolates the molecule: fibers choose between two surfaces in an otherwise identical environment. Testing two ages and two cochlear positions asks when and which fibers respond.

Tone exposure with c-fos mapping, and dye tracing

How it works

Mice hear 8 and/or 16 kHz tone pips for 90 minutes; c-fos staining marks neurons that fired. Separate dye placements trace fibers from defined cochlear spots to their CN endpoints.

Why use it

c-fos shows a physiological map, tracing shows an anatomical map. Using two different pitches shows the bands are separate in controls and overlap more in mutants.

ABR and pre-pulse inhibition

How it works

ABR uses scalp electrodes to record waves after clicks or tones: threshold shows hearing sensitivity, wave timing shows processing speed. PPI delivers a background tone with small pitch shifts before a startling noise; the more the shift reduces the startle, the better the pitch change was detected.

Why use it

PPI is a behavioral test that needs no training. The shift sizes (2 to 25%) set the difficulty so you can measure fine discrimination.

Check your understanding

Why is a normal ABR threshold important?

It shows the ear and nerve respond to sound normally, so the discrimination problem is not from hearing loss.

How is this like the retinal map?

Gradients of ephrin repellent steer fibers to their positions, giving topographic order; here the gradient is across the cochlear nucleus.

What do the later slides add?

Ephrin-B2 also repels fibers in a region-dependent way, and EphA7 mutants show altered maps, so multiple ephrin-Eph pairs likely cooperate.

The slides continue: ephrin-B2 also repels fibers in a region-dependent way (apical ones more sensitive), and early EphA7 mutants show an altered map. The model slide summarizes the idea.

Saurabh, Guerrero, Cusick, ..., Cavanaugh (2026), The FEBS Journal, doi:10.1111/febs.70631 (the PDF named fulgham_cavanaugh is this paper)

Circadian rhythms of metabolite abundance in Drosophila are largely driven by time of feeding

Many body chemicals rise and fall across a day. One explanation is that body clocks in tissues like the fat body directly run metabolism. Another is that the brain clock sets when the animal eats, and eating drives the chemical cycles. Using fruit flies, the authors remove clocks in specific tissues and find the feeding schedule is the bigger driver.

Background you need first

The big idea. Clocks run inside cells. In flies, the core loop is: CLOCK and CYCLE turn on period and timeless; PER and TIM proteins build up, enter the nucleus and shut CLOCK/CYC off; they then degrade and the cycle restarts, taking about 24 hours. Clocks exist in the brain and in most body tissues. The brain clock controls behavior, including when to eat and move. Peripheral clocks like the fat body are thought to run local functions like metabolism.

Two rival ideas. (A) The fat body clock itself drives daily cycles of metabolism, so removing it should flatten metabolite rhythms. (B) The brain clock sets feeding times, and feeding and fasting drive metabolite cycles, so removing the fat body clock should matter little but forcing a feeding schedule should matter a lot. The experiments are built to separate these.

How to separate them. Remove the clock in one tissue at a time (fat body or brain, with CRISPR). Then add a rescue-like twist: give brain-clockless flies a fixed feeding window (TRF) so they eat on a schedule again. If metabolite rhythms return, feeding time is the cause.

Key terms in this paper
Circadian clock
a roughly 24-hour molecular timer inside cells; fly core genes include period (per), timeless (tim), Clock and cycle
Central vs peripheral clock
the brain clock cells vs clocks in other tissues such as the fat body
Fat body
the fly organ like our liver plus fat tissue; stores fat and sugar and manages metabolism
Oenocytes
neighbor cells of the fat body that also handle lipids
GAL4/UAS
a genetic switch: GAL4 (the driver) decides which cells and UAS (the target) decides which gene is activated
CRISPR-Cas9 of per
gene editing that cuts the period gene, breaking the clock in only the targeted cells
CT / ZT
circadian time (in constant darkness) / zeitgeber time (relative to the light-dark cycle)
snRNA-seq
single-nucleus RNA sequencing: reads which genes are on in each individual cell nucleus
Metabolomics (GC-TOF MS)
measuring hundreds of small chemicals at once with a mass spectrometer
RAIN, BH-q
a test for 24-hour rhythms, and the false-discovery correction that guards against false positives from testing many metabolites
Time-restricted feeding (TRF)
letting animals eat only during a set window each day
Ad libitum
food available at any time

Top findings, slide by slide

1. Removing the fat body clock does not change behavior; the brain clock sets feeding

Plain version: the fat body clock is not what tells flies when to eat or move.

Why they did this: Before any metabolic conclusion, you must prove (1) the fat body clock is truly gone, (2) neighboring cells are untouched, and (3) behavior is unchanged, otherwise any metabolic change might be indirect.

How to read this slide

Antibody staining of PER in fat body cells for to>perCRISPR vs to>acpCRISPR controls, and a bar chart of the percentage of fat body cells with PER.

What it shows

PER is lost from most fat body cells in the experimental flies while the control guide leaves it. The clock is knocked out in the target tissue.

How to read this slide

Locomotor activity (left) and feeding (right) over days in constant darkness for control, fat-body-clockless and brain-clockless flies, with rhythm strength plotted.

What it shows

Fat body clock loss does not alter activity or feeding rhythms, but brain clock loss abolishes them. This confirms the brain, not the fat body, sets behavior, so changes in metabolism cannot come from changed feeding.

Putting it together: Behavior is the key control: fat-body-clockless flies eat on the normal schedule, so any metabolic differences would be due to the local clock, not feeding.

Full detail from the paper

Using to-GAL4 to drive CRISPR against period, PER protein disappeared from about 90% of fat body cells (the other driver, Lsp3.1, only 67%), while oenocytes kept it. snRNA-seq confirmed that core clock genes tim, vri and Pdp1 no longer differed between CT0 and CT12 in the fat body. These flies had normal locomotor and feeding rhythms in constant darkness. In contrast, breaking the clock in brain neurons (Clk856-GAL4) wiped out both. So behavior rhythms come from the brain.

2. The fat body clock still sets the time-of-day activity of many metabolic genes

Plain version: the fat body clock matters for gene activity even if behavior ignores it.

Why they did this: If the fat body clock is real but not needed for behavior, what does it do? Reading all genes in single cells at several time points shows whether the clock drives gene expression cycles.

How to read this slide

Bar charts of the number of rhythmic genes in fat body and oenocytes, control vs clock-less flies (JTK_CYCLE).

What it shows

Losing the fat body clock reduces the number of cycling genes in both tissues, so the clock imposes daily expression rhythms.

How to read this slide

Gene ontology chart of the processes enriched among rhythmic fat body genes.

What it shows

The cycling genes are enriched for carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, homeostasis and starvation response, fitting a role in metabolism.

How to read this slide

Counts of genes up or down in clock-less fat body and oenocytes, and example expression plots across time.

What it shows

Losing the clock changes both the level and the timing of many genes, including in neighboring oenocytes, a non-cell-autonomous effect.

Putting it together: So the fat body clock does control local gene activity. The surprise is that this barely shows up in metabolite levels, which the next finding explains.

Full detail from the paper

In control flies, 173 fat body transcripts differed between CT0 and CT12, and they were enriched for carbohydrate, lipid and glycogen metabolism. In clock-less fat body only 75 differed. Examples: Gart and Lsd-1 lost their daily difference, while bmm (the main fat-burning lipase) was reduced. The talk adds a finer analysis over 12 time points with JTK_CYCLE (a test that finds genes with 24-hour rhythms), again showing fewer rhythmic genes without the clock, with effects in oenocytes too.

3. But chemical rhythms are mostly set by when the fly eats

Plain version: feeding on a schedule creates strong chemical cycles; free feeding barely does.

Why they did this: The key test: do whole-body metabolite cycles depend on the fat body clock, the brain clock, or on eating times? The design compares four groups.

How to read this slide

The two guiding questions: how feeding rhythms are generated and how central and peripheral clocks coordinate outputs such as feeding and metabolism.

What it shows

These are the questions the experiments in findings 1 to 3 answer. The slide deck itself stops at transcriptomics, so the metabolite result is from the paper.

Putting it together: Result in the paper: with free feeding, no metabolite is significantly rhythmic in control, fat-body-clockless or brain-clockless flies. Brain-clockless flies on TRF have 43 rhythmic metabolites (sugars mid-feeding, amino acids at the end of fasting). Conclusion: feeding time is the main driver; fat body clock may instead buffer nutrient fluctuations.

Full detail from the paper

The authors measured 164 identified metabolites every 2 hours for 2 days. In flies that ate freely, whether normal, fat-body-clockless or brain-clockless, no metabolite passed the strict test (BH-q below 0.05). When brain-clockless flies were limited to a 12-hour feeding window, 43 metabolites cycled: sugars peaked mid-feeding (CT4 to 8) and amino acids late in the fast (CT20 to 24). Control flies showed weak versions of some of the same rhythms. No slide covers this part, so cite the paper.

Methods that established them

GAL4/UAS CRISPR clock knockout

How it works

GAL4 lines (to for fat body, Clk856 for brain clock cells) drive UAS-Cas9 and guide RNAs against period. The non-clock gene acp guide is a control. Staining counts cells that lost PER.

Why use it

Tissue-specific knockout lets you test each clock separately, which whole-animal clock mutants cannot do. Drawback: to-GAL4 is also active in a few non-fat-body tissues, so the authors checked PER there.

Single-nucleus RNA-seq

How it works

Abdomens are dissected, nuclei isolated, barcoded (Parse) and sequenced. Clusters are named by marker genes (fat body, oenocytes). Memento and JTK_CYCLE test genes for differences and rhythms.

Why use it

Abdomens mix many cell types; single-nucleus data let you analyze fat body separately. Drawback: the paper used two time points while the talk uses twelve.

Metabolomics, RAIN and TRF

How it works

Whole bodies sampled every 2 h over 2 days; GC-TOF mass spectrometry measures hundreds of metabolites; RAIN tests for 24 h patterns of any shape; q-values correct for many tests. TRF flies move between food and agar vials.

Why use it

Dense sampling and replicates detect rhythms; BH correction avoids false positives. Drawbacks: males only, whole body, limited chemical coverage.

Check your understanding

Why does behavior control matter for the fat body knockout?

If feeding rhythms changed, metabolic differences could be due to feeding, not the local clock. They did not change.

Why use TRF in brain-clockless flies?

These flies have no feeding rhythm. TRF gives them one; if metabolite rhythms appear, the feeding schedule is sufficient to drive them.

If the fat body clock changes gene expression, why not metabolites?

Genes may anticipate feeding to stabilize energy levels, buffering fluctuations rather than creating large daily swings.

Limits: only male flies; this method misses many lipids; whole-body samples can hide tissue-specific rhythms; the paper's snRNA-seq used only two time points.
